statement: Two-dimensional TMDCs such as MoS2 attract intense study for electronic applications.
Depositing large-area TMDC films of adequate quality under conditions that applications allow is still a major unsolved challenge.
Plasma-enhanced ALD gives polycrystalline, wafer-scale MoS2, TiS2 and WS2 films with controlled thickness at temperatures as low as 100 °C, a record low.

Keeping excess sulfur from the H2S-based plasma out of the film is what allows crystalline growth; adding H2 to the plasma feed gas achieves this (two key factors: remote H2S plasma with reactive radicals and low-energy ions, and enough H2 next to H2S, since excess S blocks crystallization).

MoSx films were characterized systematically (composition, crystallinity, growth, morphology, electrical behaviour) over a wide window of deposition conditions, showing the interplay of temperature and H2 flow ratio.
Film properties were related to the behaviour of field-effect transistors made from MoS2 deposited at 100 °C.
Deposition of MoS2 on PET substrates (and the 100 °C FET channel) points to use of the process in flexible electronics and other fields needing low deposition temperatures.

Composition control by tailoring the plasma chemistry is expected to hold for low-temperature plasma deposition of metal chalcogenides in general, including other PEALD sulfides and phase control of sulfides with several stoichiometries.
TMDCs have unusual electronic, optical and mechanical properties owing to their layered crystal structure, and are stable as single monolayers.
TMDCs are of interest for electronics, catalysis, energy storage and medicine.
The TMDC family has over 30 layered MX2 materials (M a transition metal or Sn, X being S, Se or Te), from semiconductors to (semi)metals and superconductors.
TMDC devices shown so far include FETs, photodetectors, tunneling FETs, memristors and memtransistors; semiconducting MoS2 and WS2 are studied as silicon alternatives.
Mechanically exfoliated flakes, used in early and many current TMDC studies, cannot be scaled up.
High-temperature CVD from oxide powder precursors gives high-quality TMDCs, but often struggles with large-area uniformity and thickness control, for which some fixes exist.
CVD of MoS2 typically needs 600-800 °C.
Back-end-of-line processing allows at most 400-500 °C.
Metal-organic and halide CVD and ALD processes give polycrystalline MoS2 at 200-500 °C.

TMDCs are promising for flexible electronics and displays, e.g. as thin-film transistors and as gas, light, biomolecule and pressure sensors; BEOL integration aims at memory and photodetectors on Si chips.
Typical polymer flexible substrates tolerate maximum temperatures of 100 to 400 °C.
PET should stay below 100-150 °C to avoid deforming.
The few known TMDC ALD processes at or below 150 °C give amorphous films with too little conductivity and mobility for electronics.
For plastic substrates only film transfer or assembly from flake dispersions (printing, spin coating) is available now.
Direct deposition is preferable for simplicity, cost, film quality and uniformity, and coverage of 3D structures.

PEALD reaches high film quality at low temperature through reactive radicals and low-energy ions that add energy without heating the substrate much; being self-limiting it offers uniformity, thickness control, reproducibility and scalability.
The group's earlier PEALD processes for MoS2 and WS2 work well at 300 °C and above, but below 300 °C give amorphous, S-rich, highly resistive films.
Highly conductive TiS2 has been grown by PEALD down to 150 °C.
As far as the authors know, 100 °C is the lowest temperature reported for MoS2 from any chemical vapour-phase method.
Besides stoichiometry and crystallinity, hydrogen in the feed gas also changes growth, morphology and electrical properties, together with deposition temperature (studied in detail for MoSx).
The key process parameters discussed apply to other plasma-made chalcogenides too, not only MoS2.
One ALD cycle: Mo(NtBu)2(NMe2)2 vapour pulse that reacts until surface sites are used up, purge, H2S/H2/Ar remote plasma exposure, second purge; cycles are repeated to the target thickness.
The plasma strips the ligands of the adsorbed Mo precursor and delivers S to the film.
Saturation curves show the process is self-limiting.
Plasma feed gas composition and deposition temperature together decide whether amorphous S-rich or polycrystalline MoS2 grows.
a-MoS2+x denotes amorphous S-rich films and c-MoS2 polycrystalline MoS2 films.
The H2 flow ratio is the H2 fraction of the H2 plus H2S flow in the plasma feed gas.
Eq. 1 relates the H2 flow ratio to the H2 and H2S flow rates in sccm: ratio = H2/(H2 + H2S).
Absolute flows and other process parameters are given in the Experimental Section.
At 150 °C, ratios of 0 to 0.50 give a-MoS2+x with weak, broad Raman bands resembling amorphous MoS3.
At 150 °C polycrystalline MoS2 needs a ratio of at least 0.65, seen from the appearance of the MoS2 E1g (E2g1) and A1g Raman modes.

statement: Raman peak intensity rises from ratio 0.65 to 0.80, suggesting better crystallinity.
XRD confirms crystalline films for ratios of 0.65 and above.
With the optimized ratio 0.80, crystalline MoS2 grows at 150 °C with sub-monolayer thickness control.
With more cycles the E2g1 peak moves to lower and A1g to higher wavenumber (dashed lines in the panel), confirming thickness control.
Thickness can be set by cycle number from about one monolayer to tens of nm.
Most H2-flow-ratio comparisons use films 10-20 nm thick made with 100-140 cycles.
Thickness standard deviation over a 4" wafer is 3.3% (film mean 5.1 ± 0.2 nm printed on the map).
MoS2 films about 1-5 nm thick are smooth and continuous with no visible holes by AFM.
MoS2 is deposited on PET at the lowest temperature, 100 °C, with optimized ratio 0.80.
About 5 nm MoS2 on PET has a resistivity of 0.3 Ω cm.
The 5 nm MoS2 films on PET are highly transparent and their resistivity does not change after repeated bending by hand.
The lowest H2 flow ratio giving crystalline films rises as deposition temperature falls.
At 300 °C and above even ratio 0.20 gives c-MoS2.

TEM specimen: a sub-5 nm c-MoS2 film grown at 100 °C with ratio 0.80 and 50 cycles.
The 100 °C film looks fully crystallized and is built of nanocrystallites 4-5 monolayers thick.
Nanocrystallites of the 100 °C film are about 5-10 nm wide.
Surface of the 100 °C TEM film is fairly smooth, RMS roughness 0.75 nm by AFM.
Reference TEM film grown at 350 °C with ratio 0.20 (60 cycles, reference condition after Sharma et al.).
The 5-6 monolayer film made at 350 °C has a microstructure and crystallinity much like the 100 °C film.
S/Mo atomic ratio and crystallinity are strongly correlated.
Most crystalline films have XPS compositions between MoS1.8 and MoS2.3, close to MoS2.
Right stoichiometry and chemical environment from plasma chemistry control let MoS2 crystallize at temperatures down to 100 °C.
Amorphous films grown at 150 °C or more hold excess S, MoS2.5 to MoS3.6.
Within the amorphous region, raising temperature at fixed ratio lowers S/Mo.
The lower S/Mo at higher temperature is likely due to changed reaction mechanisms and lower stability of S-rich compositions and their S2- and S2 2- species at higher temperature.
Stoichiometry and crystallinity come from the interplay of plasma chemistry (set by the H2 flow ratio) and surface chemistry (set by ratio, deposition temperature and film crystallinity).
At 50-100 °C some films made with high ratios are near MoS2 composition yet amorphous.
Those low-temperature exceptions may come from too little thermal energy to crystallize and an S environment more like a-MoS2+x than MoS2.
Ratio 0.94 gives a low S/Mo although Raman shows MoS2 peaks.
The 0.94 films hold both c-MoS2 and metallic Mo, so too high a ratio can starve the film of S and/or etch S away.
XPS core levels of 150 °C films grown with several ratios and 140 cycles are shown as examples; other temperatures are in Table S1.
In the Mo 3d region most Mo is Mo4+, assigned to MoSx.
All samples show two weaker doublets at higher binding energy: the highest is Mo6+ (MoO3) from oxidation in air after deposition, the middle one Mo5+ (MoOySx), an intermediate oxidation product.
c-MoS2 films need an extra weak doublet below Mo4+, labelled Mo(4-δ)+ and assigned to more metallic Mo at crystal edges, metastable 1T' MoS2 or MoS2-x subsulfide.
Mo 3d5/2 binding energy of the Mo(4-δ)+ component of the ratio 0.80 c-MoS2 film is 228.9 eV.
Mo 3d5/2 binding energy of the Mo4+ component of the ratio 0.80 c-MoS2 film is 229.6 eV.
Mo 3d5/2 binding energy of the Mo5+ component of the ratio 0.80 c-MoS2 film is 231.1 eV.
Mo 3d5/2 binding energy of the Mo6+ component of the ratio 0.80 c-MoS2 film is 232.9 eV.
Average literature Mo 3d5/2 binding energy of MoS2 is 229.3 ± 0.5 eV.
Average literature Mo 3d5/2 binding energy of MoO3 is 232.7 ± 0.3 eV.
Measured binding energies vary slightly with deposition conditions.
At ratio 0.94 an intense doublet below Mo4+ appears, assigned to metallic Mo.
Two S 2s singlets overlapping Mo 3d are included in the fit.
S 2p of the ratio 0.80 crystalline film fits fairly well with one S2- doublet of MoS2 at S 2p3/2 162.4 eV.
A weak doublet about 0.9 eV below the main one improves the fit; it is assigned to electron-rich S2- on metallic edges, in 1T' MoS2 or in MoS2-x subsulfide.
A doublet above the S2- one is strongest for the low-ratio amorphous films.
In the a-MoS3.0 film (ratio 0.50) the two S 2p3/2 components sit at 161.9 eV, with roughly equal area to the other.
In the ratio 0.50 amorphous film the higher S 2p3/2 component is at 163.1 eV; no electron-rich S2- is seen in this or other amorphous samples.
Amorphous MoS3 contains sulfur in at least four chemical environments.
Lower-BE S doublet = MoS2-like S2- plus terminal S2 2-; higher-BE doublet = bridging S2 2- plus apical S2-.
The varied S species and their overlapping binding energies prevent an exact determination of S species or S oxidation states.
The area ratio of the higher-BE to the lower-BE doublet grows for more S-rich material.
With Mo as Mo4+ in both MoS2 and MoS3, charge neutrality requires more S2 2- in place of S2- the more S-rich MoS2+x is, so the lower- and higher-BE doublets mainly reflect S2- and S2 2-.

RBS S/Mo ratios agree closely with XPS for the three 150 °C films.
Nitrogen left from precursor ligands is low, 0.5-1.5 at.%.
Oxygen is under 1 at.% in the ratio 0.20 and 0.65 films.
Higher O at ratio 0.80 is likely surface oxidation helped by a rough morphology with many easily oxidized edge sites, also hinted by the low mass density.
Hydrogen is the main impurity and clearly increases with the ratio, even if roughness and surface oxidation may inflate the last value.
Morphology matters: roughness can raise resistivity by carrier scattering, hinder integration in nanoscale devices, and tells about growth mechanisms.
Morphology comparisons use relatively thick films, 8-20 nm, grown with 140 cycles.
Thinner films are smoother and differ less between conditions.
At 150 °C, amorphous films from ratios 0-0.50 are very smooth by SEM and AFM.
Raising the ratio to 0.65 gives crystalline but still smooth films.
At ratio 0.80 films are rough, made of out-of-plane oriented MoS2 crystallites ('fins').
At the highest ratio 0.94 the areal fin density drops, possibly because part of the film is metallic Mo.
Other temperatures behave alike: amorphous films are smooth at every temperature, crystalline films just past the onset are fairly smooth, and roughness grows with ratio up to the roughest at 0.80.
The minimum ratio for crystalline (rougher) films falls as deposition temperature rises.
A higher ratio appears to promote fin formation and/or growth.
Out-of-plane fins are common in (PE)ALD and CVD multilayer TMDC films.
In PEALD MoS2 and WS2 the fins sit (almost only) at grain boundaries, so grain size and boundary density control fin density.
Possible fin mechanism 1: two crystallites grow sideways until they meet, then the top layer(s) of one or both bend upward into a fin.
Possible fin mechanism 2: metal precursor adsorbs at a reactive grain-boundary or defect site and nucleates a new, randomly oriented grain.
Fin edges carry more reactive sites than basal planes, so fins grow vertically faster than new basal layers form, giving the usual change from smooth to fin-dominated films with thickness.
In this process the ratio may tune edge reactivity by changing S and S-H coverage on the edges.
DFT for WS2 showed that lower S coverage and higher S-H coverage of edges favour W precursor adsorption.
A similar effect is expected here because Mo(NtBu)2(NMe2)2 has the same ligands as the W precursor and Mo and W are chemically alike.
Thick ratio-0.80 films are very rough, so fins form and grow easily under those conditions.
With ratio 0.65 at 150 °C crystalline films stay smooth even at about 50 nm (500 cycles).
By TEM, in the first ~5 nm next to the SiO2 the MoS2 grains lie about parallel to the substrate; above that crystallites are randomly oriented, yet the film is smooth and dense.
S-rich (H-poor) plasma may hinder fin growth compared with S-poor (H-rich) plasma.

The ratio at which fin growth sets in depends on temperature: at higher temperature a lower ratio suffices to activate edges, perhaps through precursor adsorption kinetics or easier excess S at low temperature.
Excess surface S at low temperature fits the need for a higher ratio to reach MoS2 stoichiometry and crystallinity at lower temperatures.
At 150 °C, in situ SE shows amorphous films from ratios 0 to 0.50 thickening linearly with cycles.
Crystalline films just past onset (0.65, 150 °C) also grow roughly linearly but with a higher GPC than amorphous ones.
Ratio 0.80 gives clearly non-linear growth with GPC rising as cycles accumulate.
Ratio 0.94 lowers the GPC again.
The lower GPC at 0.94 may reflect a mixed MoS2/Mo film whose phases differ in density, mechanism and morphology.
GPC averaged over the first 100 cycles increases from ratio 0 to 0.80 at every temperature.
Two factors explain the GPC trend: more adsorption sites for the Mo precursor at higher ratio, and more surface area and reactive fin edges at higher ratio and temperature.
By RBS, Mo atoms deposited per cycle are 0.6 at/nm2/cycle at ratio 0.20 and 150 °C.
By RBS, Mo atoms deposited per cycle rise to 1.6 at/nm2/cycle at ratio 0.65 and 150 °C, more than double, with little change in morphology.
DFT for WS2 PEALD found that the metal precursor can adsorb on -SH sites.
The density of -SH (thiol) groups, and with it the GPC and doping, should increase with the H2 flow ratio, as observed.
Fin formation and growth make GPC increase with cycle number.
GPC rising with thickness was seen for crystalline MoS2 at ≥300 °C with ratio 0.20 and in other crystalline TMDC ALD processes.
The most Mo per cycle, 2.2 at/nm2/cycle, is deposited at ratio 0.80.
Optical GPC hides density and stoichiometry changes, but SE with RBS and XPS indicates that Mo precursor adsorption density dominates the GPC trends.
At 250 °C ratios 0.35 (amorphous) and 0.50 (crystalline) give almost equal GPC.
Crystallization itself changes GPC at most moderately, less than ratio and morphology do.
The H2 flow ratio tunes resistivity over several orders of magnitude.
At a given temperature and fixed cycle count, higher ratio gives lower resistivity.
For amorphous films resistivity follows stoichiometry.
The most S-rich films (S/Mo ≥ 3) exceed the four-point probe detection limit, of order 1000 Ω cm for 10 nm films.
Lower S/Mo, from higher ratio and/or temperature, lowers resistivity.
Lowest amorphous-film resistivity is 2 Ω cm, for MoS2.2 grown at 100 °C with ratio 0.65.
For crystalline films, raising the ratio at a given temperature lowers resistivity.
Lowest c-MoS2 resistivities, about 0.1-1 Ω cm, are reached at ratio 0.80.
Crystalline film grown at 300 °C with ratio 0.20 has 15 Ω cm.
Crystalline film grown at 450 °C with ratio 0.20 has 220 Ω cm.
Ratio 0.94 gives resistivities down to 4 mΩ cm, likely owing to a highly conductive Mo phase.
c-MoS2 resistivity is lowest at the lowest temperatures, 100-150 °C.
c-MoS2 films grown with ratios 0.50-0.80 at 100-250 °C show p-type conduction with hole concentrations of order 10^21 cm^-3 by AC Hall.
Hall mobilities of these low-temperature c-MoS2 films are modest, 0.001-0.01 (cm^2/Vs).
Reference c-MoS2 films from 350-450 °C with ratio 0.20 have carrier densities of order 10^17 to 10^18 cm^-3.
Those reference films have similar or slightly higher mobilities, of order 0.01 (cm^2/Vs), here and in Vandalon et al.
Similar mobilities at 150 and 450 °C indicate comparable electronic quality.
MoS2 doped with 10 at.% Al at 450 °C has carrier concentrations and mobilities comparable to the low-temperature c-MoS2 here.
The process offers an easy way to make strongly p-doped MoS2 at low temperature.
At 450 °C, raising the ratio from 0.20 to 0.80 lifts carrier concentration 3 orders of magnitude, from 10^17 to 10^20 cm^-3.
Ratio 0.94 gives extremely high carrier concentrations, of order 10^22 cm^-3, consistent with partial Mo content.
Mo thin films have carrier concentrations of 5 × 10^22 to 1 × 10^23 cm^-3.
c-MoS2 films are near stoichiometric, MoS1.8 to MoS2.2 by XPS.
The high hole concentrations are attributed mainly to H incorporated from the plasma, H being the main impurity by RBS.
12 at.% H in the 150 °C, ratio 0.65 film corresponds to 6 × 10^21 H atoms/cm3, three times its measured carrier concentration.
N and O are far less abundant than the carriers; grain boundaries and S or Mo vacancies may also add carriers.

Literature (mostly DFT) places H in MoS2 at S vacancies (n- or p-type), on S as thiol groups (n-type), interstitially within the Mo plane (n-type), as neutral intercalated H2, or replacing S to form n-type MoSH.
Annealing up to 300 °C causes no major change in electrical properties.
Infrared and Raman measurements found no evidence of Mo-H or S-H bonds, which does not prove they are absent.
Given the process and the S deficiency of crystalline high-ratio films, H most likely sits at S vacancies or in thiol groups.
FET channel: about 5 nm film grown at 100 °C with ratio 0.80.
Reference FET film of similar thickness grown at 350 °C with ratio 0.20.
Both FETs conduct p-type with on/off current ratios of about 3-4.
Few p-type 2D semiconductors are known, unlike n-type ones.
Output current of the 100 °C FET is over ten times that of the 350 °C reference, matching its lower resistivity and higher carrier concentration.
The 100 °C FET contacts show non-linear I-V (a Schottky barrier); the 350 °C contacts are near Ohmic.
Device cross-sections show an amorphous MoS2/Ni interface layer about 2-3 nm thick for the 100 °C sample.
The 350 °C device has a thinner interface layer, about 1 nm.
The thicker interface of the 100 °C sample may explain its non-linear I-V.
Films made at 100 °C start oxidizing when annealed in air at only 150 °C.
Further work is needed on carrier density control, contact/MoS2 interfaces and MoS2 stability during processing for low-temperature PEALD MoS2.
The H2 flow ratio is a key parameter for low-temperature PEALD of TMDCs generally, allowing crystalline films at lower temperatures than before.
The group's published WS2 and TiS2 PEALD processes use H2S/Ar plasma without H2 (ratio 0) and give highly S-rich films at low temperature.
The tungsten sulfide process gives crystalline WS2 only from 300 °C.
Without H2 at 150 °C the W sulfide films are highly S-rich (WS4.0 by XPS), amorphous and highly resistive, like the analogous MoS2 films.
Ratio 0.80 at 150 °C yields crystalline WS2.1.
The crystalline WS2.1 film has a resistivity of 4 Ω cm.
MoS2 and WS2 behave alike since Mo and W share a group and both processes use analogous M(NtBu)2(NMe2)2 precursors.
The only reported TiS2 PEALD process is crystalline from 150 °C, but gives amorphous TiS3 at 100 °C.
A thermal TiS2 ALD process with the same Ti(NMe2)4 precursor grows crystalline films down to 100 °C.
So the PEALD failure at 100 °C stems from excess S rather than lack of energy for crystallization.
With ratio 0.50 at 100 °C, TiS2 has better crystallinity and stoichiometry than the reported thermal process.
For TiS2 the ratio 0.80 used for MoS2 and WS2 is too high and gives S-poor films (not shown).
OES of the H2S/H2/Ar plasma suggests S-containing species S, S+, S2, SH+ and H2S+; atomic H (H radicals) is the main reactive hydrogen species.
OES can hardly tell sulfur species apart, so changes in plasma species with ratio are hard to infer.
Combined H2S plus H2 flow is held at 10 sccm (except at ratio 0.94).
With rising ratio, atomic H emission grows while reactive S species emission falls, consistent with the flow changes.
H2S itself contains H, so some atomic H forms even with no added H2.
A higher atomic H to reactive S ratio may either keep excess S out or add a reaction that removes S.
Extra step test: a separate H2 gas or H2 plasma step follows the H2S/H2/Ar plasma (ratio 0.20) at 150 °C, conditions that otherwise give a-MoS3.4.
The H2 plasma step removes the extra S and yields c-MoS2, whereas H2 gas changes neither stoichiometry nor crystallinity.
H radicals can convert a-MoS2+x into c-MoS2 under these ALD conditions, though prevention of S uptake by a higher ratio is not excluded.
Lowering the H2S flow reduces S incorporation like raising the ratio; crystalline films form at 250 °C with no H2 added.
At lower temperature such as 150 °C, H2 addition is still needed for c-MoS2.
At fixed ratio, more H2S flow increases S incorporation.
Ratio, absolute H2 and H2S flows and deposition temperature must all be considered to get the wanted film properties.
Polycrystalline films reach compositions MoS2.2, TiS2.2 and WS2.2 (conclusions; the WS2 section gives WS2.1).
Quantifying temperature and ratio effects opens further development of low-temperature PEALD of crystalline chalcogenides with controlled stoichiometry.

Thickness is followed in situ by SE with a J.A. Woollam M-2000FI (0.8-5.0 eV; fits over 0.8-4.0 eV) or M-2000F (1.2-5.0 eV).
An in situ SE measurement is usually taken every 10 cycles.

SE optical model: MoSx (B-spline)/SiO2/interlayer/Si in CompleteEASE 5.1, with software optical constants for the other layers; roughness of crystalline MoS2 as an effective medium layer with 50% void.
Reported SE thickness = dense MoSx layer plus half the roughness layer, approximating the deposited amount.

Fitting: SiO2 thickness and substrate temperature from the spectrum before cycle 1; MoSx thickness and optical constants from the last spectrum; only MoSx thickness (and roughness) for spectra in between.
Reported thicknesses average many grains of slightly different thickness and optics over a few mm2.
Ex situ SE uses a J.A. Woollam M-2000U at 65, 75 and 85° incidence over 1.2-6.5 eV, fitting MoS2 and SiO2 thickness with fixed optical constants from in situ data.
Uniformity maps use a J.A. Woollam M-2000 (1.2-3.3 eV) with a mapping stage, circular pattern avoiding wafer edges; a 5 nm MoS2 film on a 4" 450 nm SiO2/Si wafer and a bare substrate were measured.
Sheet resistance is measured with a four-point probe (Keithley 2400 SourceMeter, Signatone SP4-4004STRS head).
Resistivity = sheet resistance × film thickness from in situ SE.
Hall measurements: van der Pauw geometry on about 1 × 1 cm2 samples (Lakeshore 8404 HMS), AC Hall for low Hall voltages, repeated without removing the sample to estimate uncertainty.
SEM: Zeiss Sigma at 3 kV with InLens detector.
AFM: Bruker Dimension Icon, PeakForce Tapping ScanAsyst mode in air, probes of 0.4 N/m nominal spring constant and 2 nm tip radius.
Rq is the root-mean-square roughness of a 500 × 500 nm2 image after first-order flattening in Nanoscope 2.0.
Raman: Renishaw inVia confocal microscope, 514 nm laser, NA 0.75 50× objective, 1800 lines/mm grating; six 10 s spectra accumulated.
Laser power on the sample is about 0.6 mW (100 mW laser through a 1% ND filter).
XPS: Thermo Scientific K-Alpha with monochromatic Al Kα (1486.6 eV) in a 400 µm spot, flood gun against charging.
Spectra are referenced to adventitious C 1s at 284.8 eV.
Pass energies: 50 eV for survey and 20 eV for high-resolution spectra.
Peaks are fitted in Avantage with Gaussian-Lorentzian sum components and a Shirley background.
XPS depth profiles (Ar+ at 500 eV, spectrum every 30 s) on selected samples showed no major carbon contamination.
RBS and ERD are done by Detect 99 B.V. with a 2 MeV He+ beam; RBS gives atom density, stoichiometry and non-H impurities, ERD gives hydrogen.
Reported RBS/ERD uncertainties include known systematic and statistical parts.
TEM lamellae are prepared by FIB lift-out (FEI Helios Nanolab 600/600i) with C/Pt or SiO2 masks and imaged on a probe-corrected JEOL ARM 200F at 200 kV.
The ~50 nm 150 °C TEM sample is used as deposited; the ~5 nm 100 and 350 °C samples first get transistor channel patterning and Au/Ni metallization.
